Leaves simple, commonly opposite and decussate with one of each pair slightly smaller than the other, rarely verticillate or alternate; venation acrodromous, with the secondary veins running from base to apex more or less parallel to the margin and the tertiary veins reticulate between them - the character by which the family is recognised in the field. Inflorescences cymose, umbellate, corymbose, in paniculate clusters or a cincinnus, rarely the flowers single, fascicled or spicate. Flowers bisexual, actinomorphic though the androecium is often slightly zygomorphic, usually (3 or)4- or 5(or 6)-merous, the perianth biseriate, perigynous. Hypanthium funnel-shaped, campanulate, cyathiform or urceolate. Calyx lobes (3-)5(or 6), valvate. Petals (3-)5(or 6), distinct, imbricate. Stamens usually twice as many as the petals in two whorls, rarely as many by loss of a whorl, isomorphic or dimorphic; filaments distinct and often geniculate, inflexed in bud; anthers typically 2-celled, introrse, basifixed, dehiscing by one or two apical pores or short longitudinal slits.

families.description: Dioecious woody or sometimes herbaceous climbers, rarely erect shrubs or trees; tubers sometimes present; sometimes producing exudate or rarely latex. Wood often with concentric rings or arcs of vascular bundles separated radially by interfascicular rays, or the bundles in one ring; wood sometimes yellow. Young shoots often tendrilliform; young stems usually drying longitudinally striate. Stipules absent. Leaves spiral, simple, often palmatinerved at the base and sometimes peltate, or penninerved, the margin usually entire and sometimes broadly crenate or deeply 3-5-lobed; petiole often swollen at the base and sometimes also at the apex, sometimes leaving a raised discoid scar on the stem. Inflorescences axillary, on defoliate branches, or cauliflorous, solitary or fascicled, often cymes, thyrses or pseudoracemes; female inflorescences usually fewer-flowered than male. Flowers small, usually green, yellow or white, actinomorphic, the female sometimes zygomorphic. Sepals usually in 1-2(-4) whorls of 3, or one whorl of 4, the outer whorls smallest, imbricate. Carpels always free, reduced to 1 in Cissampelos, Cyclea and Stephania.

families.description: Perennial or monocarpic herbs growing from sympodial rhizomes or a massive sympodial corm. Pseudostems composed of closely packed leaf sheaths. Leaves spirally arranged, petiolate; blade entire, pinnately veined, and readily tearing along the lateral veins. Inflorescence terminal or rarely axillary, cymose. Bracts spirally arranged, often brilliantly coloured, spathe-like and large. Flowers bisexual or unisexual by abortion, zygomorphic. Perianth in two whorls, the three outer tepals and two of the inner united into a compound tepal, the third inner tepal free. Stamens 5, free; anthers 2-locular. Ovary inferior, 3-locular with numerous axile ovules. Style simple. Fruit a berry, fleshy or leathery and dry, indehiscent. Seeds hard, not arillate.
families.philippine_note: CDFP accepts 10 Philippine species in 2 genera (Musa, Ensete), 2 of them endemic (20%). The bananas and abaca. Musa textilis, the source of Manila hemp, is among the most economically important plants in Philippine history.

description.text: Perennial or monocarpic herbs growing from sympodial rhizomes or a massive sympodial corm. Pseudostems composed of closely packed leaf sheaths. Leaves spirally arranged, petiolate; blade entire, pinnately veined, and readily tearing along the lateral veins. Inflorescence terminal or rarely axillary, cymose. Bracts spirally arranged, often brilliantly coloured, spathe-like and large. Flowers bisexual or unisexual by abortion, zygomorphic. Perianth in two whorls, the three outer tepals and two of the inner united into a compound tepal, the third inner tepal free. Stamens 5, free; anthers 2-locular. Ovary inferior, 3-locular with numerous axile ovules. Style simple. Fruit a berry, fleshy or leathery and dry, indehiscent. Seeds hard, not arillate.

families.description: Evergreen trees or shrubs, usually with cavities containing essential oils in the foliage, branchlets and flowers. Stipules absent or small and caducous. Leaves opposite, occasionally alternate, ternate or pseudo-whorled; blade with pinnate or basal secondary veins, often with an intramarginal vein near the margin, the margin usually entire. Inflorescences axillary or terminal, cymose but variously arranged, one- to many-flowered. Flowers bisexual and sometimes polygamous, actinomorphic. Hypanthium usually adnate to the ovary and prolonged above it. Calyx lobes (3 or)4 or 5 or more, distinct or connate into a calyptra. Petals 4 or 5, sometimes absent, distinct or connate into a calyptra. Stamens usually numerous in one to several whorls, the filaments distinct or connate into five bundles opposite the petals; anthers 2-celled, dehiscing longitudinally or rarely terminally, the connective usually ending in one or more apical glands. Ovary inferior, semi-inferior or very rarely superior, with 2 or more carpels and 1 to many locules, the placentation usually axile. Style single; stigma single. Fruit a capsule, berry, drupaceous berry or drupe. Seeds without endosperm or the endosperm sparse.

families.description: Perennial aquatic herbs. Rhizomes branched and creeping, forming swollen terminal storage tubers late in the growing season. Leaves arising from the rhizome, alternate, emersed or floating, long-petiolate; blade centrally peltate with radiating veins - the leaf is attached at its centre, not at a marginal sinus, which separates this family at a glance from the water lilies. Flowers solitary, axillary, long-pedunculate, bisexual, hypogynous, actinomorphic, borne above the water surface. Tepals numerous and distinct, the outermost reduced and the inner larger and petaloid. Stamens numerous. Pistils numerous and simple, separately and loosely embedded in cavities on the flattened top of an enlarged receptacle. Ovary 1-locular with a single pendulous ovule. Fruit nut-like and indehiscent, seated in the spongy receptacle. Seeds without endosperm or perisperm; embryo large.

families.description: Carnivorous, dioecious, woody or subwoody climbers or subshrubs, terrestrial or epiphytic. Stems terete, 2-4-angled, or winged. Buds naked, lacking scales. Leaves exstipulate, involute or convolute, marcescent, simple, chartaceous or coriaceous, petiolate or sessile; the midrib extended into an unbranched tendril whose distal part expands into an elaborate animal-trapping pitcher containing digestive fluid. Pitchers dimorphic: lower pitchers borne from rosettes or short stems, often resting on the ground, usually ovoid or globular, the mouth facing the stem, with two ventral fringed wings and a straight tendril; upper pitchers usually more elongate and infundibuliform, the mouth facing away from the stem, the wings reduced to ridges or absent, and the tendril coiled. Pitcher mouth apical or subapical, rimmed with a ribbed peristome, the inner edge often toothed and bearing nectar glands, sometimes raised at the rear into a column supporting the lid; lid usually held over the mouth, its lower surface with a laterally flattened basal appendage; spur inserted where the lid joins the pitcher. Inflorescence terminal but appearing lateral through subsequent growth, a paniculoid thyrse or raceme of 6-300 flowers. Stamens 4-12, the filaments united into an androphore and the anthers into a subspherical head. Fruit a loculicidal capsule of 4 valves with 50-500 seeds; seeds filiform, 3-25 mm long, slender through long basal and apical appendages.

families.description: Ferns whose rhizome system is composed of two distinct elements: erect, rootless, frond-bearing parts, which in all Malesian species form well-developed erect and sometimes aerial trunks bearing several green fronds at once; and creeping, root-bearing runners arising from the frond-bearing part, variously developed and branched. The vascular system of the erect part is a dictyostele, that of the runners protostelic. In some species the runners form underground tubers, irregularly globose to somewhat elongated, up to a few centimetres across and densely scaly, from which new plantlets can arise and whose water reserve is drawn on in drought. Scales most densely set on the rhizome and the basal part of the stipe, sparser on runners and stipes, and in most species very sparse or absent on the lamina of mature fronds.

families.description: Trees, shrubs, herbs, or armed climbers; roots not rarely tuberous. Indumentum of simple hairs. Leaves simple, exstipulate, opposite or rarely whorled or pseudowhorled, sometimes unequal within a pair. Inflorescence cymose, often thyrsoid, corymbose or umbellate, terminal or axillary, sometimes cauliflorous. Bracts and bracteoles present, sometimes very small and not rarely early caducous. Flowers actinomorphic, bisexual or unisexual by reduction, pedicelled with 1-3 sometimes coloured bracteoles, or subtended by an involucre. Perianth tubular, campanulate, funnel-shaped or urceolate, sometimes articulated with the pedicel; the basal part persistent, enclosing the receptacle, tubular to club- or funnel-shaped and often accrescent; the apical part mostly circumscissile and caducous, plicate or valvate in bud, with (4-)5-10 green or coloured lobes. Stamens 1-40, rarely more, in 1-2 whorls, connate at the base, free from the perianth.

families.description: Perennial or rarely annual aquatic herbs. Stems rhizomatous, the rhizomes erect or creeping. Leaves arising from the rhizome, simple, alternate, floating, emersed or submersed, long-petiolate; blade undivided, usually with a basal sinus, often peltate. Flowers solitary, axillary, long-pedunculate, bisexual, hypogynous to epigynous, actinomorphic, mostly emergent. Sepals 4-7, usually green and occasionally petaloid. Petals numerous and rarely absent, distinct, usually showy, often grading into the stamens. Stamens numerous; anthers introrse, the connective sometimes appendaged. Pistil compound of 5 to many partially or completely united carpels surrounding a sometimes projecting floral axis. Ovary multilocular with laminar placentation. Fruit a spongy berry ripening under water.

families.description: Trees or erect, rarely scandent shrubs, sometimes hemiparasitic and rarely autoparasitic. Leaves spirally arranged, rarely distichous, simple, entire, often with parchment-like and/or finely tuberculate surfaces, mostly penninerved and rarely plinerved, petioled, exstipulate, not rarely greyish-yellowish-olivaceous and dull, especially when dry. Petals 3-7, free or connate below, valvate, caducous. Disk sometimes present, of free glands or cup-like. Stamens 1-3-seriate, hypogynous, 4-15, epipetalous or partly episepalous, rarely in part staminodial; anthers basi- or medifixed, dehiscing lengthwise. Ovary mostly superior, rarely semi-inferior when immersed in the disk.

families.description: Ferns of simple morphology, the variability concentrated in the rhizome. Rhizomes short-creeping and forming compact clumps of fronds, or more widely creeping; in some species short-lived and decaying less than a metre behind each growing point, giving scattered stands, in others highly persistent and forming extensive dense stands. Parts of the rhizome may grow outwards or upwards from the substrate to form erect or drooping, often rootless aerial stems - the shrubby growth form most often associated with the genus, though it occurs in a minority of species. Branches often opposite. Fronds simple, monomorphic or slightly dimorphic, often in whorls, articulated to phyllopodia.

families.description: Small evergreen trees, shrubs or lianas; two genera, Cansjera and Opilia, are known to be root parasites. Leaves distichous, simple, usually extremely variable in form and size, entire, exstipulate, pinnately veined; dried leaves mostly finely tubercled by cystoliths in the mesophyll. Inflorescences axillary or cauliflorous, panicle-like, racemose or spicate; bracts narrowly ovate or scale-like, peltate in Opilia, often early caducous. Flowers small, (3-)4-5(-6)-merous, mainly bisexual, sometimes unisexual and the plants then dioecious or gynodioecious. Perianth of valvate, free or sometimes partly united tepals. Stamens as many as and opposite the tepals; anthers introrse, 2-celled, dehiscing longitudinally. Disk intrastaminal, lobed, annular or cupular. Ovary superior, 1-celled; style short or none; ovule 1, pendulous from the apex of a central placenta. Fruit drupaceous, the pericarp rather thin, the mesocarp fleshy-juicy, the endocarp woody or crustaceous. Seed large, conforming to the drupe, without a testa.

families.description: Perennial and sometimes short-lived herbs, terrestrial, epiphytic or lithophytic, autotrophic or rarely mycotrophic, rarely scrambling vines, with rhizomes, tubers or rootstocks, the roots bearing mycorrhizal fungi. Stems sympodial or monopodial, usually leafy but the leaves sometimes reduced to bract-like scales, one or more basal internodes often swollen into a pseudobulb; epiphytic species with aerial photosynthesising adventitious roots, these usually sheathed in one or more layers of dead cells forming a velamen. Leaves one to many, alternate or occasionally opposite, often distichous, sometimes terete or channelled, frequently fleshy or leathery, the base almost always sheathing and sometimes articulated. Inflorescence basal, lateral or terminal, erect to pendulous, racemose, spicate, subumbellate or paniculate, one- to many-flowered. Flowers small to large and often showy, usually zygomorphic, bisexual, most often resupinate with the pedicel and ovary twisted through 180 degrees. Ovary inferior, 1-locular with parietal placentation, rarely 3-locular and axile. Sepals usually free, the median often unlike the laterals, the laterals sometimes adnate to a column foot to form a saccate, conic or spur-like mentum. Petals free or rarely partly adnate to the sepals; the median petal modified into a lip, entire to variously lobed or 2-3-partite, frequently ornamented, spurred or saccate. Stamens and style united into a column.

families.description: Annual, biennial or perennial parasitic herbs, without chlorophyll in the holoparasitic genera. Stems unbranched or sometimes branched. Leaves scale-like, spirally or subimbricately arranged. Inflorescences racemose, spicate or subcapitate, rarely 1-flowered; a single bract usually resembling the leaves, with 2 bractlets adnate to the base of the calyx or pedicel. Flowers bisexual, subsessile or pedicelled. Calyx tubular, cupular or campanulate, (3 or)4-6-lobed or spathe-like, sometimes absent or of 3 free sepals. Corolla bilabiate and usually curved, sometimes tubular-campanulate or funnelform with 5 subequal lobes; upper lip entire, emarginate or 2-lobed; lower lip 3-lobed. Stamens 4, didynamous, inserted at the base of the corolla tube; anthers 2-celled, dehiscing longitudinally. Ovary superior, 1-locular with parietal placentation. Fruit a capsule with very numerous minute seeds.

families.description: Terrestrial plants with a mostly unbranched, often massive, erect or shortly creeping trunk, sometimes tree-like, clothed in roots and persistent stipe bases and hairy at the apex. Rhizome anatomy distinctive: an ectophloic siphonostele with a parenchymatous pith and phloem outside the vascular cylinder only, with a ring of discrete xylem strands, these often conduplicate in cross section. Fronds 1- or 2-pinnate, bearing wool-like uniseriate hairs when young, these deciduous or persisting on the axes; fronds dimorphic or with the fertile portions unlike the sterile; stipe caespitose and spirally arranged, with laterally winged stipules at the base. Sporangia large, not in true sori, borne on contracted fertile segments, opening by an apical slit.

families.description: Trees, shrubs or woody lianas, terrestrial, evergreen, dioecious. Stems simple or often bifurcately branched, ringed with persistent annular leaf scars, often producing adventitious prop roots. Leaves simple and numerous, spirally arranged at the apex of stems and branches - typically in three ranks, giving the twisted appearance the screw-pines are named for - sessile, linear to lanceolate, leathery, often lustrous or glaucous, keeled abaxially, parallel-veined with numerous horizontal secondary veins, the base open-sheathed and amplexicaul, the margin and abaxial midrib often spinulose, the apex often long-acuminate. Male inflorescences axillary and terminal, compound and bracteate, of several-branched racemes or panicles with crowded flowers on spicate ultimate branches; spathes often enlarged and white or coloured. Perianth absent. Male flowers sessile, the stamens numerous and fasciculate, the filaments smooth in Pandanus and papillose in Freycinetia; anthers basifixed, dehiscing by longitudinal slits. Female inflorescences terminal, solitary or in spikes, racemes or capitula, short and bracteate, often pendulous in fruit. Female flowers with or without staminodes; pistils free or aggregated and appressed into one- to many-carpelled phalanges; ovary superior, 1- to several-locular; style absent or very short. Fruit a berry in Freycinetia or a woody multiple fruit in Pandanus.

families.description: Mostly climbing herbs or lianas with axillary tendrils, rarely erect herbs, shrubs or small trees, glabrous or hairy, in Malesia not spiny. Branching usually by a supra-axillary serial bud. Leaves mostly spirally arranged, simple or compound, penninerved or palminerved, entire or lobed; petiole or blade base often with one to many glands, and glands often on the margin and lower surface of the blade. Stipules present. Inflorescences essentially axillary, cymose, sessile or peduncled, 1- to many-flowered, ending in tendrils or not. Flowers often stiped and articulate to the pedicel, actinomorphic, bisexual or functionally unisexual, or polygamous. Perianth mostly biseriate and persistent, the segments free or partially connate, inserted on the rim of a saucer-, cup-shaped or tubiform hypanthium. Sepals (4-)5(-6), imbricate. Petals (4-)5(-6), mostly imbricate. Corona inserted on the hypanthium, mostly a complicated structure of filaments, hairs or appendages, or membranous and annular, or of scales, rarely absent. Stamens 4-10, inserted mostly at the base of the hypanthium or on an androgynophore, mostly opposite the sepals.

families.description: Erect or decumbent herbs, beset with very short white mucigenous hairs and often also with much longer articulate hairs. Leaves opposite or the upper spirally arranged, the larger sometimes compound or deeply divided, the smaller simple and entire or shallowly serrate-dentate. Flowers solitary in the axils of the upper leaves, nodding, zygomorphic. Calyx persistent, small, deeply 5-partite. Corolla much exceeding the calyx, gamopetalous and mostly very oblique, the tube decurved and gradually widened upwards, subgibbous at the back of the base, with a ring of hairs inside beneath the insertion of the filaments; lobes 5, imbricate in bud, the anterior much the largest. Stamens 4, didynamous, inserted near the base of the corolla; anthers free with a bifid base, the connective gland-tipped; staminode minute or absent. Ovary 2-celled, the cells halved by a parietal radial false septum, each compartment with many uniseriate superposed ovules; stigma 2-lamellate. Capsule oblong or slightly broadened upwards, obtusely quadrangular with 4 longitudinal grooves, unarmed, dehiscing longitudinally.

families.description: Perennial, more or less succulent herbs, often somewhat woody and procumbent and rooting at the base, often clothed with branched multicellular hairs; the habit sometimes recalling certain Gesneriaceae. Leaves alternate, simple, mostly somewhat asymmetrical, sinuate-denticulate or subentire, somewhat fleshy, petiolate, exstipulate. Inflorescences axillary, cymose, often scorpioid, acropetal, solitary or 2-3 together in each axil. Bracts usually rather large and membranous. Flowers hermaphrodite, actinomorphic except for the calyx, shortly pedicelled or sessile. Calyx tube campanulate or linear-cylindric, adnate to the ovary by 5 longitudinal septa formed by the continuation of the filaments, leaving 5 deep nectariferous pits below the petals; lobes 5, imbricate, mostly membranous, persistent, unequal with 2 larger and 3 smaller, mostly whitish. Corolla inserted at the apex of the calyx tube, gamopetalous or less often choripetalous, more or less campanulate, mostly fleshy or cartilaginous, persistent, the 5 (rarely 4) segments valvate and often reflexed at the apex. Stamens 5, alternipetalous, shortly adnate to the corolla; anthers ovate to linear, introrse, basifixed, dehiscing by slits. Ovary inferior, 2-locular.

Fruit an achene or capsule.

families.description: Evergreen monoecious trees, rarely shrubs. Bark smooth to rough, especially on older trees, flaking irregularly. Long-shoot leaves linear to lanceolate, often minutely serrate and spirally placed, soon replaced by scales in whose axils arise short shoots in the form of needle bundles, each bundle enclosed at the base by a sheath of scale leaves; the adult needles linear and pungent, each needle in cross-section forming a sector of the circle formed by the whole bundle. Pollen cones numerous, axillary, cylindrical, subtended by a cluster of overlapping scales resembling the foliage bud; microsporophylls scale-like, each with two inverted pollen sacs. Seed cones terminal, woody, the fertile scale free from and not fused to its subtending bract, bearing two inverted winged seeds.
families.philippine_note: CDFP accepts 2 species of Pinus for the Philippines, neither endemic. These are the only native Philippine members of a family that is otherwise northern-temperate.

description.text: Evergreen monoecious trees, rarely shrubs. Bark smooth to rough, especially on older trees, flaking irregularly. Long-shoot leaves linear to lanceolate, often minutely serrate and spirally placed, soon replaced by scales in whose axils arise short shoots in the form of needle bundles, each bundle enclosed at the base by a sheath of scale leaves; the adult needles linear and pungent, each needle in cross-section forming a sector of the circle formed by the whole bundle. Pollen cones numerous, axillary, cylindrical, subtended by a cluster of overlapping scales resembling the foliage bud; microsporophylls scale-like, each with two inverted pollen sacs. Seed cones terminal, woody, the fertile scale free from and not fused to its subtending bract, bearing two inverted winged seeds.

families.description: Herbs, shrubs or climbers, rarely trees, usually aromatic. Vascular bundles more or less scattered in transverse section, in a monocotyledon-like manner. Tip of the stem sometimes enclosed in a stipule-like sheath (the prophyll), sometimes adnate to the petiole, absent in Peperomia. Leaves alternate, often opposite or whorled in Peperomia, simple, the base often asymmetric, palmately or pinnately veined. Inflorescence a pedunculate spike, rarely grouped into an umbel or a raceme, leaf-opposed or axillary, rarely terminal. Flowers small, bisexual, polygamous or dioecious, nearly always sessile; bracts small and usually peltate or cupular; perianth absent. Stamens 1-10, the filaments usually free; anthers 2-locular, dehiscing longitudinally. Gynoecium of 2-5 connate carpels; ovary superior, 1-locular with a single orthotropous ovule; stigmas 1-5, sessile or on very short styles. Fruit a small drupe or nutlet, the pericarp fleshy or dry, sometimes with sticky papillae in Peperomia. Seeds with copious starchy perisperm and a minute embryo.

families.order_source: PPG I (2016) -- Pteridophyte Phylogeny Group I, 'A community-derived classification for extant lycophytes and ferns', Journal of Systematics and Evolution 54:563-603. NOT stated by CDFP, which provides no order-level classification for pteridophytes on its own site.
families.description: Terrestrial ferns, small to medium-sized, 10-150 cm and rarely to 2 m high, entirely devoid of scales. Rhizome stout and thickened with persistent stipe bases, erect to suberect or short-decumbent, dictyostelic, sometimes bifurcate or stoloniferous; roots blackish, sparsely branched, wiry, regularly arranged on the stem with one beside each stipe base. Fronds dimorphous, bearing minute uniseriate multicellular gland-headed mucilage-secreting trichomes, most of which are lost on drying. Stipes round, oval, triangular or tetragonal, with or without aerophores; the base swollen, flat on the ventral face and with a strong median ridge on the dorsal face dividing it into two surfaces, each bearing a row of warts resembling aerophores; stipe with a single vascular bundle expanding or dividing into three meristeles in the enlarged base. Lamina of sterile fronds herbaceous to subcoriaceous, once pinnate or deeply pinnatifid; pinnae falcate to linear-lanceolate.
families.philippine_note: CDFP accepts 7 Philippine species of Plagiogyria, none endemic. The complete absence of scales is unusual among ferns and is diagnostic here.

families.description: Herbs or small shrubs, rarely arborescent. Stipules absent. Leaves spirally alternate and usually in a basal rosette, rarely opposite or whorled, simple; blade with (1 or)3-11 arcuate veins. Inflorescences spikes, rarely racemes or 1-flowered, pedunculate, each flower with one bract. Flowers small, protogynous, bisexual, rarely polygamous or unisexual. Calyx usually 4-parted, persistent, the segments imbricate. Corolla scarious or membranous, gamopetalous, actinomorphic or rarely zygomorphic, (3 or)4-lobed, the lobes imbricate. Stamens (1 or 2 or)4, inserted on the corolla tube and alternating with the lobes; anthers free and versatile with an apical appendage. Pistil of 2 carpels; ovary superior, (1 or)2-locular; style 1, filiform. Fruit a circumscissile capsule or a nutlet.
families.philippine_note: CDFP accepts 27 Philippine species in 14 genera (Limnophila, Veronica, Adenosma, Bacopa, Plantago, Angelonia, Bythophyton, Callitriche, Digitalis, Dopatrium, Ellisiophyllum, Hemiphragma, Scoparia, Stemodia), 2 of them endemic (7.4%). This key follows the broad circumscription in which many former Scrophulariaceae are brought into Plantaginaceae, so the Philippine representation is more varied than the rosette-forming plantains alone.

families.description: Annual or perennial herbs, or tall woody bamboos. Flowering stems (culms) jointed, the internodes hollow or solid; branches arising singly from the nodes and subtended by a leaf sheath and a 2-keeled prophyll, often fascicled in bamboos. Leaves alternate in two ranks, differentiated into sheath, blade, and an adaxial erect appendage (the ligule) at the sheath-blade junction; sheath surrounding and supporting the culm internode, split to the base or infrequently tubular, modified with a reduced blade in bamboos as culm sheaths; blades usually long, narrow and flat but varying from inrolled and filiform to ovate, the veins parallel and sometimes cross-connected, especially in bamboos; ligule membranous or a line of hairs. Inflorescence terminal or axillary, an open, contracted or spike-like panicle, or of lax to spike-like racemes along an elongate axis, or digitate, paired or solitary. Spikelets of distichous bracts along a slender axis (the rachilla), the two lowest bracts (glumes) typically empty and subtending one to many florets. Florets of two opposing bracts enclosing a single small flower, the outer (lemma) clasping the more delicate, usually 2-keeled inner bract (palea); the floret base often with a thickened callus articulated with the rachilla; lemma often with an apical or dorsal awn. Flowers bisexual or unisexual; lodicules 2, rarely 3 or absent, 3 to many in bamboos; stamens usually 3, the anthers versatile; ovary 1-celled, the styles usually 2 with feathery stigmas. Fruit normally a dry indehiscent caryopsis with the pericarp firmly adherent to the seed, rarely free, fleshy in some bamboos.

families.description: Monoecious or dioecious trees and shrubs, a few prostrate (one extralimital genus parasitic on another member of the family). Cotyledons usually two, each a fused pair with a correspondingly bifid tip, occasionally more. Foliage buds ranging from a loose cluster of reduced leaves to a complex specialised structure in Podocarpus. Leaves of many shapes and sizes. Pollen cones small, with numerous microsporophylls, each bearing two inverted dorsal pollen sacs below a small sterile tip; the cones solitary in the axils of ordinary leaves, or terminal or clustered on specialised scaly structures, or occasionally in the axils of scales at the base of a new shoot. Pollen with two or more bladders, more than two only in Dacrycarpus among Malesian genera. The seed-bearing structure is a compound terminal or lateral cone in which fertile scales arise in the axils of cone bracts, often subtended by a scaly shoot or a naked peduncle. The fertile scale, or epimatium, is a highly modified shoot bearing a single naked ovule on its upper surface, inverted in most genera; it cups the developing seed and may nearly enclose it, leaving only the micropyle exposed at pollination. Fleshiness of the cone bracts, of the fertile scale, or of both is common, and the whole seed-bearing structure may be reduced to one or a few fertile units, yielding plum-like fruits.

families.description: Herbs, sometimes saprophytic, shrubs, lianas or trees. Stipules absent, but the stem sometimes with a pair of glands at the nodes. Leaves simple, entire, usually spirally arranged, sometimes alternate, semi-decussate or verticillate, sometimes scale-like or absent. Inflorescence usually raceme-like and unbranched, axillary and/or terminal, sometimes thyrsoid or fascicled, rarely the flowers solitary. Bracts present; bracteoles basal, rarely absent. Flowers bisexual, more or less zygomorphic and rarely actinomorphic. Sepals 5, free and quincuncial, or the lower two connate or sometimes all connate, subequal or the lateral ones larger and then often wing-like and petaloid. Petals 3 or 5, free or variously united and occasionally united with the calyx, usually adnate to the base of the staminal tube or the filaments, subequal or more often unequal with the lower petal often keel-like and frequently pouched, lobed or crested. Stamens 2-10, usually 8, the filaments usually more or less connate except between the upper stamens and often adnate to the petals; anthers basifixed.
families.philippine_note: CDFP accepts 29 Philippine species in 5 genera (Polygala, Xanthophyllum, Securidaca, Epirixanthes, Salomonia), 5 of them endemic (17.2%). 2%). description.text: Herbs, sometimes saprophytic, shrubs, lianas or trees. Stipules absent, but the stem sometimes with a pair of glands at the nodes. Leaves simple, entire, usually spirally arranged, sometimes alternate, semi-decussate or verticillate, sometimes scale-like or absent. Inflorescence usually raceme-like and unbranched, axillary and/or terminal, sometimes thyrsoid or fascicled, rarely the flowers solitary. Bracts present; bracteoles basal, rarely absent. Flowers bisexual, more or less zygomorphic and rarely actinomorphic. Sepals 5, free and quincuncial, or the lower two connate or sometimes all connate, subequal or the lateral ones larger and then often wing-like and petaloid. Petals 3 or 5, free or variously united and occasionally united with the calyx, usually adnate to the base of the staminal tube or the filaments, subequal or more often unequal with the lower petal often keel-like and frequently pouched, lobed or crested. Stamens 2-10, usually 8, the filaments usually more or less connate except between the upper stamens and often adnate to the petals; anthers basifixed.

families.description: Herbs, shrubs or small trees, sometimes monoecious or dioecious. Stems erect, prostrate, twining or scandent, often with swollen nodes, striate, grooved or prickly. Leaves simple, alternate and rarely opposite or whorled, petiolate or subsessile; stipules often united into a sheath around the stem (the ocrea) - the defining character of the family. Inflorescence terminal or axillary, spicate, racemose, paniculate or capitate. Flowers small, actinomorphic, bisexual and rarely unisexual. Perianth 3-6-merous in one or two series, herbaceous, often enlarging in fruit or with the inner tepals enlarged and bearing wings, tubercles or spines. Stamens usually (3-)6-9; filaments free or united at the base; disk annular and often lobed. Ovary superior, 1-locular; styles 2 or 3. Fruit a trigonous or lenticular achene, usually enclosed in the persistent perianth.

families.description: Rhizome creeping, dorsiventral, with two alternating dorsal rows of phyllopods and two alternating lateral rows of buds; scales basifixed, pseudopeltate to peltate, clathrate or isotoechous, the margin entire to ciliate. Ground tissue parenchymatous or rarely sclerenchymatous, with or without strands of sclerified cells; stele dictyostelic, of 3 to many vascular strands. Fronds often dimorphic, articulated to the phyllopods, sessile to stipitate, erect or appressed, simple to pinnate, pedately or dichotomously divided, rarely bipinnatifid, often covered with deciduous or persistent scales or hairs. Veins forked, free in a few genera to copiously branched and anastomosing. Fertile areas often contracted and frequently on separate fronds. Sori exindusiate, rounded, transversely or longitudinally elongated, or forming irregular acrostichoid patches.

families.description: Annual or perennial herbs, erect, ascending or prostrate, less than 1.5 m high. Leaves spirally arranged or alternate, often in a basal rosette, or opposite, exstipulate, simple, sometimes lobed, penninerved, often various on one plant. Inflorescences racemose, in terminal or sometimes axillary racemes or umbels, or the flowers in whorls or solitary and axillary. Bracts small or leafy; bracteoles absent. Flowers bisexual, actinomorphic and rarely zygomorphic, isomerous, in Malesia always 5-merous, often dimorphous in the sexual organs. Calyx dentate or cleft, persistent, sometimes leafy. Corolla connate, shallowly to deeply cleft, often quincuncial or contorted in bud. Stamens inserted on the corolla, epipetalous, rarely alternating with staminodes; anthers dorsifixed or versatile, sometimes basifixed, the cells opening by apical pores or latrorsely; filaments free or connate. Disk absent. Ovary superior, semi-inferior in Samolus, 1-celled with many ovules on a free central placenta; style simple. Capsule mostly 5-valved.

families.description: Small to medium-sized plants, epiphytic or on rocks. Rhizomes creeping, brown, bearing rhizoids; ROOTS ABSENT - the character that sets this family apart from every other Philippine vascular plant. Stems erect or pendulous, green, unbranched or dichotomously to pinnately branched, the branches ridged, sulcate or flattened. Leaves small or rudimentary, with a single vein or lacking veins entirely, spirally or distichously alternate, sessile, dimorphic: the sterile scale-like and subulate-triangular to lanceolate, the fertile deeply bifid. Sporangia appearing solitary at or above the bases of the fertile leaves, large, 2- or 3-lobed and sometimes interpreted as synangia, thick-walled, lacking an annulus, each lobe dehiscing longitudinally. Spores all of one kind.
families.philippine_note: CDFP accepts 3 Philippine species in 2 genera (Psilotum, Tmesipteris), 1 of them endemic (33.3%). PPG I (2016) moves Psilotaceae out of Copeland's "Lycopodineae" grouping into the ferns proper, which is one of the reasons the pteridophyte section of this key was rebuilt rather than inherited.

families.description: Parasitic plants, rootless, without chlorophyll, always rich in tannins, monoecious or dioecious. Endophytic body consisting of strings or plates of cells within the host plant. Flowering buds or flowering branches vascularised, bursting through the cortex of the host and terminating in a single flower or in short racemes or spikes, with a series of scale-like bracts at the base of the buds. Flowers unisexual or bisexual; perianth single, often tubular or saucer-shaped at the base, in Rafflesia and Sapria the apex of the tube partly closed by a diaphragm; stamens grouped around a central column that represents part of the pistil in female and bisexual flowers, and often joined to it; ovary unilocular, generally inferior, with 4-6 or numerous parietal placentas. Fruit berry-like. Seeds minute, surrounded by pulp, the testa hard and often thickened and pitted, the embryo few-celled and undifferentiated.
families.philippine_note: CDFP accepts 14 Philippine species, ALL of them endemic, all in Rafflesia. Every one carries a DENR threatened-species listing. Of the roughly 40 species in the family worldwide, the Philippines therefore holds about a third, all found nowhere else - among the most striking endemic concentrations in the flora.
families.caveat: The key reaches this family through its parasitic, rootless, leafless habit rather than through ordinary vegetative characters, which is why the description above leads with habit rather than with leaves.

families.description: Perennial or annual herbs, sometimes subshrubs or herbaceous to woody vines. Leaves basal and cauline, alternate and rarely opposite or whorled, simple or variously compound, palmately nerved and rarely penninerved, with or without stipules. Inflorescence a simple or compound monochasium or dichasium, a simple or compound raceme, or the flowers solitary. Flowers bisexual and sometimes unisexual, actinomorphic and rarely zygomorphic, hypogynous. Sepals 3-6 or more, free, petaloid or sepaloid, imbricate or sometimes valvate in bud. Petals present or absent, 2-8 or more, free, usually with nectaries. Stamens numerous and rarely few, free, some sometimes becoming staminodes. Carpels numerous to few, rarely 1, free. Fruit a head of achenes or follicles, rarely a berry or capsule.

families.description: Annual to perennial herbs, rarely woody. Leaves alternate, entire to pinnatifid, with small glandular stipules. Flowers bisexual and rarely unisexual, in terminal racemes or spikes. Sepals 4-7, persistent. Petals usually 4-7 or absent, entire or cleft, hypogynous or perigynous. Stamens 3-40, inserted on a disk and exposed in bud, the disk often eccentric; filaments free or connate at the base. Carpels 2-6, free or united into a 1-locular ovary with parietal or basal placentation; ovules numerous. Fruit a capsule, often open at the apex even before maturity, or berry-like. Seeds numerous, reniform or suborbicular; endosperm almost absent.

families.description: Terrestrial or epilithic, evergreen, medium-sized plants. Rhizome erect or creeping, the apex and stipe bases scaly, the scales brown, lanceolate, entire and long; fronds caespitose, rarely distant. Fertile fronds up to 2 m; stipe pale stramineous and usually as long as the lamina, the base not thickened, with sparse scales and glabrous above. Pinnae alternate, ascending, stipitate; pinnules anadromous with an asymmetrical or more or less symmetrical base. Sori elongate along the veins, with a membranous indusium.

families.description: Evergreen trees or shrubs, the mangrove species with various remarkable root formations. Branching in the mangrove genera mostly sympodial; branchlets swollen at the nodes, solid and pithy, hollow in Crossostylis, Gynotroches and Pellacalyx. Innovation continuous, but flushwise in Anisophyllea. Leaves decussate. Stamens as many as or twice as many as the petals, in Kandelia indefinite in number, in some species some aborted and staminodial, free or connate at the base; anthers typically 4-celled.
families.philippine_note: CDFP accepts 17 Philippine species in 7 genera (Bruguiera, Rhizophora, Pellacalyx, Carallia, Ceriops, Gynotroches, Kandelia), none endemic. Rhizophora, Bruguiera and Ceriops are the backbone of Philippine mangrove forest, and their stilt roots, knee roots and viviparous propagules are what the key uses to reach the family.
families.caveat: The extracted text is fragmented between the vegetative opening and the androecium; the leaf, stipule and fruit characters - including the viviparous seedling of the mangrove genera, which is the family's most conspicuous feature - must be completed from the printed treatment.

families.description: Trees, shrubs, annual or perennial herbs, subshrubs, vines or lianas, infrequently creeping and rooting at the nodes, terrestrial or infrequently epiphytic; flowers usually bisexual, infrequently dioecious or rarely polygamo-dioecious or monoecious; evergreen or sometimes deciduous; sometimes armed with straight to curved spines formed from modified stems or peduncles; branchlets terete to angled or quadrate. Leaves opposite or whorled, simple, the margin usually entire; stipules interpetiolar or intrapetiolar, present throughout the family and one of its defining characters, free or fused into a sheath, sometimes leaf-like, persistent or deciduous. Inflorescences terminal or axillary, cymose and variously arranged into panicles, corymbs, heads or fascicles, or the flowers solitary. Flowers usually bisexual, actinomorphic, mostly 4- or 5-merous, epigynous. Calyx limb usually developed into a tube or cup, sometimes with one lobe enlarged and petaloid. Corolla sympetalous, salverform, funnelform, campanulate or rotate, the lobes valvate, imbricate or contorted. Stamens as many as the corolla lobes and alternating with them, inserted in the corolla tube. Ovary inferior, usually 2-locular; style one, the stigma entire to variously lobed. Fruit a capsule, berry, drupe or schizocarp.

families.description: Perennial or annual plants of saline, brackish or extremely hard water, totally submerged. Rhizomes slender, usually branched. Stems terete. Leaves alternate, sessile, narrowly linear, entire or minutely denticulate toward the apex; stipules adnate to the leaf base and sheathing the stem, the sheaths shortly auriculate; ligule absent. Inflorescences few-flowered pedunculate spikes, at first enclosed by involucral leaves, the peduncles short at first and elongating - often spiralling - in fruit. Flowers hermaphrodite, small, ebracteate. Perianth absent. Stamens 2, the anthers sessile and extrorse. Carpels 4 or more, free, 1-ovuled, sessile in flower but usually becoming narrowly stipitate in fruit; stigma sessile, peltate or umbonate. Fruit drupaceous and asymmetric, borne on a slender stalk.

families.description: Aquatic plants forming floating mats; roots present in Azolla and lacking in Salvinia; stems horizontal, vegetative reproduction rapid by fragmentation. In Salvinia the fronds are in whorls of three, the upper surface covered with water-repellent papillae: two fronds float and are green with an orbicular to oblong lamina 8-25 mm long, while the third is submersed, finely dissected and root-like. Sporangia are contained within sporocarps borne on the submersed frond. Heterosporous.

families.description: Trees, shrubs or lianas, rarely herbaceous climbers; monoecious, rarely dioecious or polygamous. Indumentum usually of solitary simple hairs, sometimes also of two-branched hairs, stellate bundles, or scale hairs, the young parts then viscid. Leaves spirally arranged, rarely opposite or whorled, simple, biternate, digitate or (bi)pinnate; true stipules usually absent, pseudo-stipules sometimes present. Leaflets alternate to opposite, symmetric to distinctly asymmetric, entire to dentate, serrate or crenate. Inflorescences axillary and often together pseudoterminal, or terminal or ramiflorous, thyrsoid; bracts and bracteoles present. Flowers usually unisexual, rarely bisexual, actinomorphic or zygomorphic. Sepals 4 or 5, rarely more, free to almost wholly connate, equal to distinctly unequal. Petals absent or 2-6, free, usually clawed, often with 1 or 2 scales or auricles. Disc complete or interrupted, lobed or annular to semi-annular. Stamens 5-10(-74), usually 8, nearly always inserted within the disc, often exserted in male flowers; anthers basifixed, opening lengthwise. Ovary superior, 1-3(-8)-celled; style usually apical; ovules 1 or 2 per locule. Fruit capsular or drupaceous, or of 2 or 3 samaras; capsules usually loculicidal. Seeds globose to obovoid, sometimes compressed, often with an arillode or sarcotesta; endosperm absent.

description.text: Herbs or shrubs, rarely trees or vines. Leaves simple or compound, usually alternate or opposite, usually exstipulate. Flowers usually in cymes, panicles or racemes, rarely solitary, usually bisexual, hypogynous to more or less epigynous and rarely perigynous, actinomorphic and rarely zygomorphic, 4- or 5(-10)-merous. Sepals sometimes petal-like. Petals usually free, sometimes absent. Stamens (4 or)5-10 or many, the filaments free; staminodes often present. Carpels 2, rarely 3-5(-10), usually more or less connate; ovary superior to inferior, 2- or 3-5(-10)-locular with axile placentation, or 1-locular with parietal placentation; ovules usually many. Fruit a capsule or follicle.

families.description: Woody vines, monoecious or dioecious. Leaves alternate or somewhat clustered, exstipulate, petiolate; lamina simple. Flowers generally solitary and axillary to the leaves on ultimate branches, or in the axils of fugacious bracts near the base of ultimate shoots, occasionally paired or in clusters of up to 8, unisexual, hypogynous, pedicellate, with few to numerous generally spirally arranged parts. Perianth segments free, not differentiated into distinct sepals and petals, the outermost and innermost sometimes reduced.

families.description: Herbs, sometimes shrubs, rarely trees, mostly autotrophic and less often hemiparasitic or parasitic. Stipules absent. Leaves alternate, opposite, whorled, or opposite below and alternate above, simple or sometimes pinnately dissected. Inflorescences racemes, spikes or thyrsoid panicles, or the flowers solitary. Flowers bisexual, usually zygomorphic and rarely actinomorphic. Calyx often persistent, (2-)4- or 5-lobed, variously connate. Corolla sympetalous, the limb (3 or)4- or 5-lobed and often 2-lipped. Stamens mostly 4 and didynamous, sometimes with 1 or 2 staminodes, less often 2 or 5; anther locules 1 or 2, free or confluent. Nectary often present at the ovary base. Ovary superior, 2-locular. Fruit usually a capsule with numerous small seeds.

families.description: Herbs, shrubs, small trees or climbers. Stems sometimes prickly, rarely thorny; hairs simple, branched or stellate, sometimes glandular. Leaves alternate, solitary or paired, simple or pinnately compound, without stipules; blade entire, dentate, lobed or divided. Inflorescences terminal but overtopped by the continuing axis so as to appear axillary, extra-axillary or leaf-opposed, often apparently umbellate, racemose, paniculate or clustered, or the flowers solitary, rarely true cymes. Flowers mostly bisexual, usually regular, 5-merous and rarely 4- or 6-9-merous. Calyx mostly lobed, often persistent and enlarging in fruit. Petals united. Stamens as many as the corolla lobes and alternating with them, inserted within the corolla; anthers dehiscing longitudinally or by apical pores. Ovary superior, usually 2-locular with axile placentation. Fruit a berry or capsule.

families.description: Trees or shrubs, rarely herbs or lianas; young growth usually stellately hairy; bark mucilaginous and rich in fibres. Leaves alternate; stipules usually present and caducous; blade simple and rarely palmately compound, entire, serrate or parted. Inflorescence axillary or rarely terminal, paniculate, corymbose, racemose or cymose, rarely solitary. Flowers unisexual, bisexual or polygamous. Sepals (3-)5, more or less connate and rarely free, valvate. Petals 5 or lacking, free or adnate to the base of the androecium, convolutely imbricate. Androgynophore usually present; filaments usually connate into a single tube; staminodes 5, tongue-like or filiform and opposite the sepals, sometimes lacking; anthers 2-celled. Pistil of 2-5(or 10-12) more or less connate carpels. Fruit usually a capsule or of follicles, sometimes woody.

families.description: Evergreen trees or shrubs. Leaves simple, spirally arranged and sometimes pseudo-alternate, the margin entire or toothed, mostly with a stellate or lepidote indumentum. Stipules absent. Flowers bisexual, actinomorphic, axillary or terminal. Calyx tubular, more or less adnate to the ovary; lobes, where present, valvate. Corolla rarely of free petals, mostly united into a basal tube, 4-7-lobed, valvate or imbricate. Stamens equal to and alternating with the petals, or double their number, mostly adnate to the tube. Disk absent; anthers 2-celled, introrse, splitting lengthwise. Ovary superior, rarely semi-inferior, 3-5-celled. Style 1; stigma punctiform to 3-5-lobed.

Corolla rarely of free petals, mostly united into a basal tube, 4-7-lobed, valvate or imbricate. Stamens equal to and alternating with the petals, or double their number, mostly adnate to the tube. Disk absent; anthers 2-celled, introrse, splitting lengthwise. Ovary superior, rarely semi-inferior, 3-5-celled. Style 1; stigma punctiform to 3-5-lobed.

families.description: Trees or shrubs. Leaves alternate, simple or pinnately compound; stipules small or absent. families.description: Terrestrial, erect, perennial, mostly rosulate, scapose herbs. Rhizome tuberous, solid, starchy, globose or elongate, either with apical growth or with spaced growing points. families.description: Evergreen trees or prostrate shrubs. Bark thin, smooth, purple-red, peeling in large thin flakes. Leaves spirally placed but usually twisted into a single plane, linear to linear-lanceolate, acute, distinctly constricted at the base where the leaf twists into a horizontal position and widening again in the decurrent part; a single vascular strand marked beneath by a blunt ridge separating two bands of stomata, and above by a sharp narrow ridge on a stomata-free surface. Foliage and fertile buds small and globular, of several small keeled overlapping scales. Usually dioecious, the fertile structures borne in the axils of ordinary leaves. Pollen cone solitary above a basal cluster of sterile scales, each peltate microsporophyll with a symmetrical whorl of 6-8 inverted pollen sacs. Seed-bearing structure compound, of one or more short ovule-bearing shoots on a very short fertile axis; a small basal aril grows gradually to cup the single erect terminal seed, finally becoming fleshy and bright red. Mature seed flask-shaped.
families.philippine_note: CDFP accepts a single species of Taxus for the Philippines, not endemic.
families.caveat: The fleshy covering here is an aril that cups an erect seed, which is what separates this family from Podocarpaceae at couplet 26 of the key; the Podocarpaceae covering is an epimatium or receptacle of different origin.

Flora Malesiana has never treated this family - confirmed against Flora Malesiana's own list of families treated in published volumes. families.description: Large deciduous trees, often buttressed, with soft wood, dioecious. Leaves alternate, long-petiolate; blade simple, pubescent, lepidote, palmately 3-5-veined, the margin entire or dentate. Female flowers with an inferior ovary. Fruit a capsule with very numerous minute seeds.

families.description: Shrubs or trees, evergreen or rarely deciduous, usually bisexual, rarely dioecious in Eurya or androdioecious in Ternstroemia. Stipules absent. Leaves simple, alternate, petiolate or rarely sessile; blade with pinnate secondary veins, the margin usually serrate and rarely entire. Flowers axillary or subterminal, solitary or sometimes up to 3 or more in a cluster or raceme, pedicellate or subsessile. Bracteoles 2-8 or rarely more, persistent or caducous, sometimes undifferentiated from the sepals. Sepals 5(or 6) or rarely more, persistent. Petals 5 or rarely more, white, red or yellow, basally connate or rarely distinct, adnate to the androecium. Stamens numerous in 1-6 whorls, the outer filaments more or less connate at the base; anthers dorsifixed or basifixed, 2-locular. Ovary superior, 3-5-locular. Fruit a capsule or berry.

families.description: Caudex erect, short-creeping or long-creeping, rarely scandent; vascular structure in all cases a radially symmetrical dictyostele. Scales usually thin, not peltate, in almost all cases bearing both marginal and superficial unicellular hairs, these either acicular or glandular. families.description: Annual or perennial herbs. Roots sometimes tuberous. Stems more or less succulent, often climbing. Stipules sometimes present, especially in seedlings. Leaves alternate, long-petiolate; blade peltate or palmately lobed or divided. Inflorescences indeterminate and racemose, or condensed and umbellate, each flower subtended by a single leaf. Flowers bisexual, solitary, zygomorphic, large, on a long axillary pedicel. Sepals 5, imbricate, the adaxial one (or three) extended into a long slender nectariferous spur. Petals 5 or some aborted, yellow, orange, blue or purple, clawed and imbricate, the two upper larger and connate with the spur. Stamens 8 in two whorls, distinct and unequal; anthers 2-celled. Fruit a schizocarp of three one-seeded mericarps.

families.description: Herbs, subshrubs or shrubs, rarely trees, very rarely climbing; stems often fibrous and sometimes succulent, sometimes armed with stinging hairs; epidermal cells of the leaves, and sometimes of stems and perianths, mostly with prominent punctiform to linear cystoliths. Leaves alternate or opposite, simple; stipules present, rarely absent. Inflorescences cymose, paniculate, racemose, spicate or cluster-capitate, usually formed from glomerules, sometimes crowded on a common enlarged cup-like or discoid receptacle, rarely reduced to a single flower. Flowers unisexual with the plants monoecious or dioecious, rarely bisexual, actinomorphic, very small, (1-)4- or 5-merous. Calyx absent; perianth lobes imbricate or valvate. Male flowers with stamens as many as and opposite the perianth lobes, the filaments inflexed in bud and springing outwards at anthesis; a rudimentary ovary often present. Female flowers with the perianth lobes free or connate and usually enlarged and persistent in fruit; ovary 1-locular with a solitary erect basal ovule; style simple or absent; stigma capitate, penicillate, subulate, filiform, ligulate or peltate. Fruit usually a dry achene, sometimes a fleshy drupe, often enclosed by the persistent perianth.
families.philippine_note: CDFP accepts 188 Philippine species in 24 genera (Elatostema, Pilea, Leucosyke, Elatostematoides, Boehmeria, Dendrocnide, Procris, Pipturus, Pouzolzia, Poikilospermum, Cypholophus, Laportea, Nothocnide, Oreocnide, Astrothalamus, Cecropia, Chamabainia, Debregeasia, Girardinia, Lecanthus, Maoutia, Musanga, Neodistemon, Urtica), 132 of them endemic (70.2%). The cystoliths and the inflexed filaments that spring outwards at anthesis are the family characters most useful in the field, and both hold in Philippine material.

description.text: Herbs, subshrubs or shrubs, rarely trees, very rarely climbing; stems often fibrous and sometimes succulent, sometimes armed with stinging hairs; epidermal cells of the leaves, and sometimes of stems and perianths, mostly with prominent punctiform to linear cystoliths. Leaves alternate or opposite, simple; stipules present, rarely absent. Inflorescences cymose, paniculate, racemose, spicate or cluster-capitate, usually formed from glomerules, sometimes crowded on a common enlarged cup-like or discoid receptacle, rarely reduced to a single flower. Flowers unisexual with the plants monoecious or dioecious, rarely bisexual, actinomorphic, very small, (1-)4- or 5-merous. Calyx absent; perianth lobes imbricate or valvate. Male flowers with stamens as many as and opposite the perianth lobes, the filaments inflexed in bud and springing outwards at anthesis; a rudimentary ovary often present. Female flowers with the perianth lobes free or connate and usually enlarged and persistent in fruit; ovary 1-locular with a solitary erect basal ovule; style simple or absent; stigma capitate, penicillate, subulate, filiform, ligulate or peltate. Fruit usually a dry achene, sometimes a fleshy drupe, often enclosed by the persistent perianth.

families.description: Shrubs or trees, sometimes climbing shrubs, rarely herbs. Indumentum of simple, stellate and other complex hairs. Leaves opposite or rarely whorled, without stipules, simple or 3-foliolate, less often palmately compound. Inflorescences terminal or axillary, racemose, cymose, spicate or thyrsoid. Flowers bisexual or polygamous by abortion, zygomorphic and rarely actinomorphic. Calyx persistent. Corolla 4- or 5- or more lobed, the lobes usually spreading with overlapping aestivation. Fertile stamens inserted on the corolla tube and alternating with the lobes; filaments free; anthers dorsifixed, dehiscing by longitudinal slits or sometimes a circular pore. Ovary entire or 4-grooved, 2-8-locular with 1 or 2 ovules per locule. Fruit a drupe or a schizocarp of nutlets.

Inflorescences terminal panicles, or umbellate, spicate or capitate cymes. Flowers bisexual; calyx and corolla both connate, (3-)5-merous. families.description: Woody climbers, sometimes vines, rarely small succulent trees, hermaphroditic or polygamo-monoecious to polygamo-dioecious. Stems unarmed, sometimes with conspicuous lenticels or shredding bark; branches often swollen at the 3-7-lacunar nodes; pith continuous or interrupted by diaphragms at the nodes; tendrils simple, bifurcate to trifurcate or 4-12-branched, usually leaf-opposed, rarely absent. Raphide sacs present in the parenchymatous tissues. Leaves simple and lobed or unlobed, or digitately to pedately compound or 1-3-pinnately compound, alternate and distichous, variously toothed, commonly with multicellular stalked caducous spherical "pearl" glands; stipules 2, often caducous, or rarely absent. Flowers small, in panicles, corymbs or rarely spikes, often leaf-opposed, pseudo-terminal or axillary, actinomorphic, hypogynous, 4- or 5-merous. Calyx of 4 or 5 small teeth or lobes, or a continuous ring. Petals valvate, free or basally connate, or distally connate into a calyptra as in Vitis. Stamens 4 or 5, antepetalous; anthers introrse, dehiscing longitudinally. Floral disk intrastaminal, ring-shaped, cupular or gland-shaped. Ovary superior, 2-locular with 2 ovules per locule; style simple; stigma discoid or capitate, rarely 4-lobed in Tetrastigma. Fruit a berry with 1-4 seeds.

families.description: Perennial terrestrial and rarely epiphytic aromatic herbs with fleshy, tuberous or non-tuberous rhizomes, often with tuber-bearing roots. Stems usually short and replaced by pseudostems formed of leaf sheaths. Leaves distichous, simple, those toward the plant base usually reduced to bladeless sheaths; leaf sheath open; ligule usually present; petiole present or not, between blade and sheath; blade suborbicular to lanceolate or narrowly strap-shaped, rolled longitudinally in bud, the midvein prominent and the lateral veins numerous, pinnate and parallel, the margin entire. Inflorescence terminal on the pseudostem or on separate short sheath-covered shoots arising directly from the rhizome, cylindric, fusiform or sometimes globose, lax to dense; bracts and bracteoles present, often conspicuous and coloured. Flowers bisexual, epigynous, zygomorphic. Calyx usually tubular, thin, split down one side, the apex 3-toothed. Corolla tubular below, 3-lobed above. Stamens or staminodes 6 in two whorls: the two lateral staminodes of the outer whorl petaloid or reduced to teeth or absent, the median staminode of the outer whorl always reduced, the labellum formed from the two lateral staminodes of the inner whorl, and a single fertile stamen from the inner whorl; anther locules 2, introrse, the connective often extended into basal spurs or an apical crest. Ovary inferior, initially 3-locular.

104 of these (78.8%) are endemic to the Philippines.

Philippine genera (20), with accepted Philippine species: Adelmeria (9), Alpinia (28), Amomum (2), Boesenbergia (5), Burbidgea (1), Curcuma (2), Etlingera (21), Geocharis (1), Globba (7), Hedychium (3), Hellwigia (3), Hornstedtia (9), Kaempferia (2), Leptosolena (1), Meistera (3), Plagiostachys (10), Sulettaria (1), Vanoverberghia (5), Wurfbainia (5), Zingiber (14).
Genera endemic to the Philippines: Adelmeria, Leptosolena.
Of the accepted species, 11 are recorded as naturalized.
CDFP additionally lists 3 as cultivated but not naturalised, 11 as incertae sedis, 2 as excluded from the Philippine flora and 1 as possibly present; these are not counted in the totals above.

philippine_distribution.text: Recorded from 42 named islands or island groups; most species are reported from Luzon (73), Mindanao (67), Panay (33), Samar (30) and Negros (27).
philippine_distribution.note: Island/island-group tokens are those CDFP prints in capitals in each species' Distribution line.

philippine_distribution.text: Elevations given by CDFP for this family in the Philippines span 0–2300 m (from the 109 species for which an elevation is stated).

families.description: Prostrate hairy herbs. Leaves opposite, paripinnate, mostly anisophyllous; stipules present. Flowers actinomorphic, 5-merous, bisexual, solitary on pseudo-axillary peduncles, white or yellow. Sepals 5, free, imbricate, persistent or caducous. Petals 5, free, patent, imbricate, fugacious. Disk present. Stamens 10, subequal or unequal; anthers dorsifixed. Ovary superior, sessile, hairy, 5-12-lobed and 5-12-celled; style short and thick with 5-12 decurrent stigmas; cells with 3 or more ovules. Fruit 5-angled or 5-12-winged, the cocci partly abortive, spinous or tuberculate, indehiscent, with 3-5 superposed seeds separated by septa.
families.philippine_note: CDFP accepts 1 Philippine species in 1 genus (Tribulus), none endemic. Flora Malesiana notes the spinous fruits adhere to passing animals, which is how this genus of dry regions has spread so widely; in the Philippines it is a plant of sandy coasts and waste ground.
families.scope_note: Flora Malesiana places the morphology under Tribulus, the only genus in the Philippines.
